results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 63 aligned summaries match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01-p63) in the spec's order, including Vertical Differences after the worked example; the five opening callouts are preview/thesis callouts with no spec paragraph.

Introduction KEY POINTS callout (marked two_ideas): it is the declared thesis statement in three bullets (introduction.thesis_statement placement), not a body paragraph; its bullets are the parts of one claim. Pass.

Capability, Value Stream, Product, System ¶7 (p14, marked two_ideas): the closing sentence 'That is also why only the map answers Ingrid's question' draws the consequence of the paragraph's single idea (capabilities must be named first, and only a map names them), exactly as p14's controlling idea joins them. Pass.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene and terms to C1, map to C2, value streams to C3, heat map and Keybridge to C4, public record and worked example to the verdict claims, verticals to C2, closing sections to the method's governance.

Figures 1-5 each carry a caption saying what they show; each table is introduced or followed by a sentence reading it (level-2 table, level-3 table read by the 'machinery generic, content specific' paragraph, stream table, bottleneck table by the bold-cells paragraph, verdict table by 'The last row...', heat-map table by 'Reading the map', vertical table by 'At Veldmark this explains both', trade-off table by the Veldmark paragraph); every quotation is followed by what it shows.

Every section and paragraph transition_in is expressed at its boundary (e.g. 'Unlike the public record, Veldmark's case has a whole map', 'Those failures are mostly governance failures', 'Those decisions become questions for a review', 'The last row is the one maps forget'). The public-record opener is weak in wording and is recorded under flow_is_followable, but it does carry over the method and introduce the documented cases.

results.quote: Both need the capabilities named before anyone draws a team or a service, and the map names them.
results.finding: Reader A had to work out whether 'Both' means Lewis and Fowler's microservices and Conway's law or the two halves of 'a bargain', and found 'bargain' vague until two sentences later; the referent of 'Both' is ambiguous.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'Both need the capabilities named...' (took a re-read to settle what 'Both' refers to)

results.draft_locus: A Three-Level Capability Map for Listing Marketplaces ¶3 (identity placement bullet)
results.quote: Generic marketplace reference models make the same split
results.finding: Reference models are cited before the author's two reference models are introduced (p21), so the reader cannot tell whether these are the same models or published industry ones: a forward reference.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'Generic marketplace reference models make the same split' (which reference models is unclear at this point)

results.draft_locus: A Three-Level Capability Map for Listing Marketplaces ¶7
results.quote: They describe no real company and are cut into five root groups, not ten areas.
results.finding: The sudden first-person introduction of the Productscape models, with 'five root groups' and '88 capability slots', is never related to the chapter's ten areas and 54 level-2 capabilities ('slot' is undefined, and Reader A could not make the breakdown add up to 88); both readers stopped to reconcile the two structures.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'I maintain two generic reference models built with Productscape' (how 88 slots in five groups relate to the 10 areas and 54 level-2 capabilities is never stated)

results.draft_locus: Value Streams: Where Capabilities Meet Outcomes ¶6 (second caution)
results.quote: One of my two reference models, in parts generated by a tool rather than written by hand
results.finding: The fact that the reference models are partly tool-generated (and the 'customer jobs' layer) arrives in an aside, changing how the earlier models read; later sentences ('The tool-generated parts of those models', 'the tool-generated parts of my reference models') depend on it from far away.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'One of my two reference models, in parts generated by a tool...' (tool-generated is new here; 'customer jobs' unmentioned; later references depend on the aside)

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Shows ¶1
results.quote: The public record does show the reasoning that capability maps are used for, and its limits, though without a map; the Veldmark example that follows has one.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this sentence: 'its limits' can attach to the reasoning or the record, and the clause order ('though without a map; ... has one') is hard to parse.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'No marketplace group has published its capability map...' (had to re-read to parse 'its limits' and what 'has one' refers to)

results.quote: The program's list put media high.
results.finding: The scene's program list reads 'a group identity, trust and safety, media, ...', so trust and safety already precedes media; the claim that leadership 'moved the shared trust-and-safety platform forward' past media appears to contradict the scene. Either the scene list must say it is not the priority order (or put media earlier), or this paragraph must say what 'high' meant.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'The program's list put media high.' (trust and safety already ahead of media in the scene list; went back to check)

results.quote: Two of Veldmark's heat-map results turned on the vertical, a verdict and a score, and such results can be predicted.
results.finding: The appositive 'a verdict and a score' is awkward and does not say which verdict and which score until after the table; both readers re-read the section's opening sentence.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'Two of Veldmark's heat-map results turned on the vertical...' (awkward appositive; re-read before it became clear)

results.draft_locus: Trade-offs: Ways to Build a Capability Map ¶2
results.quote: Veldmark combined the first and third: a reference model for the skeleton, value streams to test and weight it
results.finding: The worked example's three weeks mention the reference models and the systems inventory but never show value streams being used to test and weight the map, so this summary claims a step the reader was not shown.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item 'Veldmark combined the first and third...' (the three-week description never says value streams were used)

results.quote: The second, once the group agrees on the words, is nearly identical for all four.
results.finding: The claim that the bike's capabilities are nearly identical in all four brands includes Keybridge, an agent CRM sold as software, which would not run moderation or saved searches for a city bike listing; both readers stumbled over a CRM counting as one of the four comparable marketplace brands. (That Keybridge exists is known from the preface; the problem is the claim's scope.)
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b: item on Keybridge as the fourth brand ('would a CRM need content moderation and saved searches for a city bike?')

results.quote: Two of Veldmark's heat-map results turned on the vertical
results.finding: Reader B marks the section's position 'partly unclear': its substance continues the earlier 'One skeleton, many verticals' subsection and interrupts the move from the worked example into the practitioner sections. Reader A marks it 'mostly clear' (reason given). Not corroborated; the order is the spec's declared, reasoned order.
